data.title: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis — viva
data.summary: Oral & mucosal disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Recurrent aphthous stomatitis** (Oral & mucosal disorders)_

**Q1. Define recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS).**
- Commonest oral mucosal disease: recurrent, painful, round/oval ulcers with a yellow-grey fibrinous base and erythematous halo on non-keratinised mucosa, in otherwise healthy people; affects ~20% of population; starts in childhood/adolescence

**Q2. Classify RAS.**
- Minor (Mikulicz) aphthae ~80%: <1 cm, 1–5 ulcers, heal in 7–14 days without scar
- Major (Sutton's, periadenitis mucosa necrotica recurrens) ~10%: >1 cm, deep, last 2–6 weeks, heal with scarring, can involve soft palate, fauces, tongue
- Herpetiform ~10%: crops of 10–100 pinpoint ulcers that coalesce, heal in 1–2 weeks; not caused by HSV
- Simple vs complex aphthosis (almost constant ulcers — look for systemic disease)

**Q3. Aetiology / precipitating factors.**
- Genetic predisposition (family history), local trauma (brushing, dental appliances), stress, hormonal (luteal phase), smoking cessation, food hypersensitivity (chocolate, nuts, tomato, cinnamon), sodium lauryl sulphate toothpaste
- Nutritional deficiencies: iron, vitamin B12, folate, zinc, vitamin D
- Systemic associations (aphthous-like ulcers): Behçet's disease, coeliac disease, Crohn's disease/UC, HIV, cyclic neutropenia, PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis), MAGIC syndrome, Sweet syndrome, drugs (NSAIDs, nicorandil, methotrexate, beta-blockers, mTOR inhibitors)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis of oral ulcers.**
- Herpetic stomatitis/recurrent intraoral herpes (keratinised mucosa — hard palate, gums; vesicles first)
- Hand-foot-mouth disease, herpangina, traumatic ulcer, Behçet's disease, pemphigus vulgaris, mucous membrane pemphigoid, erosive LP, EM/SJS, SLE (palatal, painless), tuberculosis, syphilis, deep fungal, SCC (persistent, indurated — biopsy any ulcer >3 weeks), drug (nicorandil), neutropenia, agranulocytosis

**Q5. What is Behçet's disease? Criteria.**
- Variable-vessel vasculitis along the old Silk Road (Turkey, Middle East, Japan); HLA-B51
- International Criteria for Behçet's Disease (ICBD 2014): oral aphthosis 2, genital aphthosis 2, ocular lesions (uveitis, retinal vasculitis) 2, skin lesions (pseudofolliculitis, erythema nodosum) 1, neurological 1, vascular (thrombosis, aneurysm) 1, positive pathergy test 1 — ≥4 points = Behçet's
- Pathergy test: 20–22 G needle prick on forearm → papule/pustule at 48 h
- Treatment: colchicine, topical steroids, apremilast (oral ulcers), azathioprine, TNF inhibitors (eye, vascular, neuro), interferon-α

**Q6. Investigations in recurrent/complex aphthae.**
- CBC, serum ferritin, B12, folate, zinc, vitamin D; coeliac serology (tTG-IgA), HIV; stool/endoscopy if GI symptoms; serial neutrophil counts for cyclic neutropenia; biopsy for atypical/persistent ulcers; pathergy and eye exam if Behçet's suspected

**Q7. Treatment.**
- Avoid triggers (SLS toothpaste, trauma, offending foods); correct deficiencies
- Topical: corticosteroids (triamcinolone in orabase, clobetasol gel, betamethasone mouthwash, beclomethasone spray), anaesthetics (lignocaine gel, benzydamine), antiseptics (chlorhexidine 0.2%), tetracycline/doxycycline mouthwash (herpetiform), amlexanox, sucralfate, hyaluronic acid gel
- Systemic (severe/major/complex): colchicine 0.5–1.5 mg/day, dapsone, pentoxifylline, short prednisolone course, apremilast, thalidomide (major aphthae in HIV — teratogenic, neuropathy), TNF inhibitors for refractory/ Behçet's
- Laser (low-level/CO2) for pain relief

**Q8. Prognosis.**
- Minor aphthae become less frequent with age; major aphthae chronic; look for systemic disease when ulcers are complex or start in adulthood

**Q9. What is the pathogenesis?**
- Immune dysregulation — T-cell (CD8 cytotoxic, Th1 — TNF-α) mediated destruction of oral epithelium, triggered by trauma, microbial antigens (streptococcal HSP), stress, hormones, nutritional deficiencies; genetic predisposition (HLA, cytokine polymorphisms)

**Q10. Oral ulcer in HIV — differential and management.**
- Major aphthae (large, painful), HSV, CMV (biopsy), histoplasmosis, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma, necrotising gingivitis; thalidomide (major aphthae), topical/ intralesional steroids, treat infections, optimise ART

**Q11. What is MAGIC syndrome?**
- Mouth And Genital ulcers with Inflamed Cartilage — overlap of Behçet's disease and relapsing polychondritis

**Q12. Treatment of Behçet's disease in detail.**
- Mucocutaneous: topical steroids, colchicine (0.5–1.5 mg/day — EN and genital ulcers), apremilast 30 mg BD (oral ulcers), dapsone, thalidomide
- Eye: azathioprine, cyclosporine, TNF inhibitors (infliximab/ adalimumab), interferon-α
- Vascular/ neuro: high-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide/ TNF inhibitors; anticoagulation controversial in venous thrombosis

**Q13. Oral lesions of nutritional deficiency.**
- Iron: angular cheilitis, atrophic glossitis; B12/ folate: beefy red tongue, aphthae; riboflavin: magenta tongue; niacin: red swollen tongue (pellagra); zinc: erosive stomatitis; vitamin C: bleeding swollen gums (scurvy)

**Q14. Histopathology of an aphthous ulcer.**
- Non-specific ulcer with fibrinopurulent membrane, mixed inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, neutrophils), perivascular lymphocytes at the edge; no viral cytopathic effect, no granulomas, no vasculitis — biopsy mainly to exclude other causes

**Q15. What is PFAPA syndrome?**
- Periodic Fever, Aphthous stomatitis, Pharyngitis and cervical Adenitis — children <5 y; episodes every 3–8 weeks lasting 3–6 days; normal growth; single dose of prednisolone aborts attacks; tonsillectomy can cure; colchicine prophylaxis

## Quick spotter facts
- Round shallow yellow-based ulcers with red halo on non-keratinised mucosa — aphthae
- Oral + genital ulcers + uveitis + pathergy — Behçet's
- Any oral ulcer >3 weeks — biopsy

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Oral mucosal disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
